title: Digital Connectivity
text:
Farm internet speeds remain among the lowest in the country despite increasing dependence on digital services.



Access to services is increasingly digital. From healthcare and education to banking and government services, many everyday activities now depend on a reliable internet connection.
Communities with poor connectivity may face barriers to participation in modern society.





Farming postcodes consistently recorded poorer internet connectivity than urban areas and generally performed worse than surrounding rural settlements, particularly when looking at higher-speed broadband services.






Note



Farm internet speeds remain among the lowest in the country despite increasing dependence on digital services.








Measure
Urban (%)
Rural (%)
Farm (%)




Above USO
99.95
98.67
96.87


Access to ≥30 Mb/s
97.94
86.46
68.51


Gigabit Availability
87.67
58.14
47.53



The largest differences emerge when considering access to high-speed and gigabit-capable broadband.



Access to broadband appears closely linked to infrastructure. Urban areas benefit from greater coverage, while connectivity decreases in more remote and dispersed settlements.
Farms often occupy the most geographically isolated locations and experience lower access to faster services.



The analysis suggests that broad urban-rural classifications may mask important differences within rural areas.
Farming communities often experience poorer connectivity than neighbouring villages despite both being classified as rural.



Spatial analysis identified significant clustering of broadband performance.



Indicator
Moran’s I




Above USO
0.373


≥30 Mb/s
0.567


Gigabit Availability
0.637



Areas with good connectivity tend to be near other well-connected areas, while poorly connected areas also cluster geographically.




Official statistics already show a rural-urban divide in connectivity.
Our findings suggest that some communities within rural areas, particularly farming households, may experience even greater disadvantage than broader rural averages suggest.
As services continue to move online, poor connectivity may reduce access to:

Healthcare
Education
Employment
Government services
Social participation










Important



There is currently no open national register of farm properties in the UK.


This analysis therefore identifies likely farming locations using a combination of:

OpenStreetMap
Companies House records

Other limitations include:

Use of postcode centroids rather than boundaries
Postcode-level broadband data
No comparable mobile coverage data at postcode scale




Future work could explore:

Deprivation and digital exclusion
Mobile connectivity
Household-level analysis through UPRN linkage
Distance to telecommunications infrastructure
Standardised UK-wide urban/rural classifications

title: Methods
text:
The ADR GIS Atlas is built on a set of reusable analytical workflows for processing administrative, geographic and environmental data.
These methods are shared to improve transparency, reproducibility and collaboration across projects.




Identification and cleaning of active postcode records using the ONS Postcode Directory.
Used for:

Geographic linkage
Address validation
Postcode matching







Classification of postcodes and locations using official rural and urban definitions.
Used for:

Population segmentation
Service accessibility analysis
Environmental modelling

Rural Urban Classification




Methods for linking postcodes, administrative boundaries and geographic datasets.
Used for:

Small area statistics
Nearest-neighbour analysis
Service catchments

Spatial Linking




Identifying locations based on open data, using Open Street Map and Companies House data.
Used for:

Finding places of interest - in this case farms

Active Postcodes




Reusable workflows for data aggregation, summary statistics and analytical outputs.
Used for:

Project reporting
Exploratory analysis
Data quality checking

Statistical Pipelines




Methods for producing location-based summaries using hexagonal grids.
Used for:

Spatial visualisation
Coverage analysis
Density estimation

Hex Grid Analysis





Where possible, methods pages include:

Data sources
Assumptions
Processing steps
Selected code examples
Links to source notebooks
Links to GitHub repositories

Code examples are presented in a condensed format to highlight the key analytical steps while keeping pages readable for non-technical collaborators.

title: ADR GIS Atlas
text:
Using linked administrative data to understand people, place, services, environment and health across Wales.
The ADR GIS Atlas brings together research, methods, interactive analyses and publications developed through spatial analysis of linked administrative data.




Research exploring inequalities in access to infrastructure and essential services.
Explore Access to Services
Current stories include:

Access to WiFi





Research examining the relationship between people, places and environmental conditions.
Explore Climate & Environment
Areas of interest include:

Environmental exposure
Climate vulnerability
Place-based inequalities





Research exploring health outcomes and inequalities through linked administrative data.
Explore Population Health
Areas of interest include:

Health inequalities
Population wellbeing
Geographic variation in health outcomes








Access to reliable internet is increasingly essential for education, employment, healthcare and social participation.
This project investigates patterns of internet and WiFi access across communities and population groups.
Explore Access to Wifi





All projects are supported by transparent and reproducible analytical workflows.
Methods documentation includes:

Data sources
Geographic processing
Statistical methods
Reproducibility guidance

Explore Methods




Publications, reports, preprints and presentations associated with Atlas projects.
Explore Publications




Feedback, discussion and collaboration are welcomed.
The Atlas is intended as a living resource that brings together research outputs, exploratory analyses, methods and data stories in a single place.
